descs.t: Abdul El-Sayed's campaign has asked Rep. Haley Stevens to stay away from all of its events in the closing days of the Michigan Senate race, according to NBC News, Politico and CNN. The split follows a clash over Israel and an ad Stevens wanted him to condemn. We walk through what each side says and what it means for the race against Mike Rogers.

The Democratic nominee for Senate in Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed, has shut his former primary rival Haley Stevens out of his final campaign events after she demanded he answer for his criticism of Israel and an ad critics call antisemitic. With Mike Rogers and even Joe Manchin pressing the point, we look at whether this fight changes the race.

Haley Stevens asked Abdul El-Sayed to condemn an ad critics call blatantly antisemitic. Instead his campaign asked her to stay away from every remaining event in the Michigan Senate race. We break down the ad, the demand, the reaction from both parties, and why this fight over Israel lands days before Michigan votes.

intro.plain: Big news out of Michigan. Abdul El-Sayed's Senate campaign has asked Haley Stevens, his own former primary rival, to stay away from all his remaining events. This comes after she pushed him over Israel and an ad she wanted him to condemn. It is days before the vote against Mike Rogers. Chat, does a public split like this move voters, or does nobody care?
intro.mid: Michigan's Democrats are fighting each other days before the Senate vote. Haley Stevens demanded Abdul El-Sayed answer for his criticism of Israel and an ad critics call antisemitic. His answer: stay away from my campaign. Mike Rogers is calling her courageous, Joe Manchin is backing Rogers. Chat, who comes out of this stronger, El-Sayed or Stevens?
intro.bold: A Democrat asked her party's Senate nominee to condemn an ad critics call antisemitic, and got locked out of his campaign for it. That is where Michigan is, days before the vote. Abdul El-Sayed's team told Haley Stevens to stay away from every remaining event. Chat, should a candidate who will not condemn that ad be anywhere near the Senate?

hook.plain: Days before Michigan votes, the Democratic Senate nominee has told his own former rival to stay away from his campaign. Here is what she asked for, and why he said no.
hook.mid: Haley Stevens wanted Abdul El-Sayed to answer for an ad and his words on Israel. His campaign asked her to skip every remaining event. Here is what that split means for Michigan.
hook.bold: She asked him to condemn an ad critics call antisemitic. He locked her out of his campaign instead. This is the fight over Israel splitting Michigan's Democrats days before the vote.

descs.t: Secretary of State Marco Rubio says the US has yet to decide on new strikes on the Islamic Republic, while reports say Washington has told Persian Gulf allies to prepare for a possible new round after November 3rd. We go through what Rubio, Trump and the regime's own commanders are saying, and what is confirmed versus reported.

Trump says the war with the Islamic Republic will end soon, a deal is being pushed, and reports say Persian Gulf allies have been told to prepare for more strikes after the midterms. Rubio says nothing is decided. We weigh the deal against the strikes and what each would mean for the regime.

The Islamic Republic says it will strike first if it sees an attack coming, and a deal is being pushed on Washington. Marco Rubio says the US has not decided on new strikes yet. We make the case for why a deal now would throw the regime a lifeline, and what keeping the pressure on could achieve.

descs.t: Texas early voting reached 6,851,810 through Friday night, according to the Secretary of State's numbers, well past the roughly 5.1 million early votes of 2022. We look at what the surge could mean for the Senate race between Ken Paxton and James Talarico and the governor's race between Greg Abbott and Gina Hinojosa.

Republicans call Texas the red wall, and early turnout of 6,851,810 has both parties watching it closely ahead of Tuesday. JD Vance and Trump are pushing Ken Paxton, while some voters say gas and grocery prices are moving them toward James Talarico. We go through who the surge may help.

Texas voters have already cast 6,851,810 early ballots, far past 2022, and the Senate fight between Ken Paxton and James Talarico is being called a race with national stakes. We break down the numbers, the voters switching sides, and what happens to the Senate map if Texas does not hold.

intro.plain: Texas is turning out. The Secretary of State's numbers show 6,851,810 Texans voted early through Friday night. The whole 2022 early vote was about 5.1 million. That is the backdrop for Ken Paxton against James Talarico for Senate on Tuesday. Chat, if you are in Texas, how long were the lines where you voted?
intro.mid: Republicans keep calling Texas the red wall. Right now 6,851,810 Texans have voted early, way past 2022. JD Vance and Trump are all in for Ken Paxton, and some voters say prices are pushing them toward James Talarico. Chat, does a turnout surge like this help Paxton or Talarico?
intro.bold: Texas is voting like the country depends on it. 6,851,810 early votes already, compared with about 5.1 million in all of 2022. Paxton against Talarico is now a Senate race both parties are scared of. Chat, straight answer: does Texas hold on Tuesday?

descs.t: US Attorney Michael Heyman and FBI Anchorage have confirmed a criminal investigation and a civil case into the second Dan Sullivan on Alaska's Senate ballot, a candidate critics call a decoy. A federal judge has also barred the federal government from trying to separate ballots in the race. We go through what has been confirmed and what is still claimed.

Republicans say Mary Peltola's side put a look-alike Dan Sullivan on Alaska's Senate ballot to confuse voters; Peltola says she never wanted that. Now federal investigators are involved, with a criminal case and a civil case confirmed. We look at the claims on each side and what it means days before Alaska votes.

A second Dan Sullivan sits on Alaska's Senate ballot, and federal investigators now have a criminal case and a civil case open over how he got there. Critics call it a decoy scheme to trick voters. We break down the evidence so far, the court fight over ballots, and why using a name to confuse voters strikes at the heart of a fair vote.

intro.plain: Alaska news. US Attorney Michael Heyman and FBI Anchorage say they have a criminal investigation and a civil case open into the second Dan Sullivan on the Senate ballot, a candidate critics call a decoy. A federal judge also ruled on how ballots are handled. Chat, would you have noticed two Dan Sullivans on your ballot?

Peltola says she never wanted it. Investigators have confirmed a criminal case and a civil case. Chat, who do you think is behind the second name?
intro.bold: Put a second candidate with the same name on the ballot and hope voters pick the wrong one. That is what critics say happened in Alaska, and federal investigators now have a criminal case open. Chat, if this is proven, what should happen to whoever planned it?

descs.t: Brazil has summoned an Argentine diplomat over the Argentine role in Flávio Bolsonaro's flight to the US, Reuters reports, citing sources. Bolsonaro left days after losing the presidential race and is set to lose his parliamentary immunity next year. We go through what is known about his departure and the investigations he faces.

Flávio Bolsonaro says he can speak more freely from outside Brazil; his critics say he is under criminal investigation for corruption. Now Brazil has summoned an Argentine diplomat over how he got to the US. We look at both claims and what the fight means for Brazil and its neighbour.

Days after losing Brazil's presidential race, Flávio Bolsonaro was in the US, and Brazil has now summoned an Argentine diplomat over the role an Argentine diplomat played. We break down his escape, the corruption investigations critics point to, his claim that he can only speak freely from abroad, and what Lula's government does next.

descs.t: Polish President Karol Nawrocki has entered the Constitutional Tribunal and challenged judges appointed by Donald Tusk's camp, after Judge Anna Korwin-Piotrowska moved to suspend the tribunal's president and vice president. Riot police contained protesters outside the court. We go through what each side says happened and what the rules say.

Supporters of President Karol Nawrocki call it a coup attempt by Prime Minister Donald Tusk; Tusk's side says it is a lawful order against a tribunal chief blocking elected judges. Riot police were outside Poland's Constitutional Tribunal as the president went in. We lay out both claims and what is at stake for the courts.

A judge ordered the leaders of Poland's Constitutional Tribunal suspended, riot police ringed the court, and President Karol Nawrocki walked in to face the judges himself. We break down the night, the coup accusations against Donald Tusk, his side's answer, and why a fight over who controls the courts matters for every free country.

intro.plain: Big night in Poland. President Karol Nawrocki went into the Constitutional Tribunal and challenged judges appointed by Donald Tusk's camp, after one judge moved to suspend the tribunal's leaders. Riot police contained protesters outside. Chat, when a government and a president fight over the top court, who should have the final word?

Tusk's side says it is a lawful order. And the president walked in to face the judges. Chat, coup or court order, which is it?
